Learning Objectives

Degenerative spondylolisthesis
Degenerative spondylolisthesis is a degenerative condition that results from arthritic changes
in the intervertebral disk space and facet joint.
Degenerative spondylolisthesis may result in back pain, pseudoclaudication, and/or radicular
leg pain from associated stenosis.
Forward slippage typically will not exceed 30% of the sagittal diameter of the vertebral body.

Overview
Degenerative spondylolisthesis is the anterior translation of a cephalad vertebral body
relative to its adjacent caudal vertebra (Figure 1). Primary spondylolisthesis is a
degenerative condition that results from arthritic changes in the intervertebral disk
space and facet joints. Secondary spondylolisthesis typically occurs adjacent to a prior
fusion.
Degenerative spondylolisthesis may result in back pain, neurogenic claudication
(pseudoclaudication), and/or radicular leg pain from associated stenosis. Forward
slippage typically will not exceed 30% of the sagittal diameter of the vertebral body.
Degenerative spondylolisthesis, often occurring in combination with spinal stenosis, is
one of the most common pathologies observed in a spine surgery practice. Primary
degenerative spondylolisthesis is defined as that occurring in patients without prior
surgical treatment. Secondary spondylolisthesis is a condition that typically occurs at the
level or levels adjacent to a prior fusion. An understanding of the basic pathophysiology
and diagnosis of degenerative spondylolisthesis is imperative to formulate an
appropriate treatment plan (Resource 1).

Epidemiology
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:35 PM
AAOS | Lumbar Degenerative Spondylolisthesis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003015
3/17

The incidence of degenerative spondylolisthesis in the general population is 4% to 6%.
Degenerative spondylolisthesis occurs 6 to 10 times more often in women than in men.
It occurs five to six times more frequently at L4-L5 than at other levels and is associated with
sacralization of L5.
Etiology
The etiology of degenerative spondylolisthesis typically is multifactorial and includes the
following1:
Degenerative changes or spondylosis
Facet arthropathy
Disk degeneration
Synovial cyst formation
Clinical Presentation
Patients typically have symptomatic spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication.

Clinical Presentation
Hallmark symptoms include neurogenic claudication exacerbated by prolonged standing
or walking. Neurogenic claudication typically is relieved by lumbar spine flexion (sitting,
supine). Patients typically do not exhibit symptoms while sitting or lying supine.
Patients with dynamic degenerative spondylolisthesis appear to experience greater
discrepancy in symptoms between erect and supine postures. Back pain and
radiculopathy may accompany symptoms of neurogenic claudication.
Classification
The Meyerding classification is most often used classification system.2 Spondylolisthesis is
classified from grade I to grade V depending on the fraction of the anterior slip relative to the
anteroposterior diameter of the caudal vertebral body (Figure 2).

Grade I: zero to 25% translation
Grade II: 26% to 50% translation
Grade III: 51% to 75% translation
Grade IV: 76% to 100% translation
Grade V: spondyloptosis
Figure 2 Illustrations show the Meyerding classification of spondylolisthesis. The numbers 1
through 4 in each image denote the fraction of the slip anteriorly. For example, Grade I = 1/4
(25%). A, Normal vertebral alignment. B, Grade I, zero to 25% translation. C, Grade II, 26% to
50% translation. D, Grade III, 51% to 75% translation. E, Grade IV, 76% to 100% translation. F,
Grade V, spondyloptosis. (Reproduced from Khalil JG, Fischgrund JS, Roberts RV: Lumbar
stenosis and degenerative spondylolisthesis, in Truumees E, Prather H, eds: Orthopaedic
Knowledge Update: Spine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons,
2017, pp 253-264.)
Physical Examination
The physical examination findings often are normal or nonspecific.
Hamstring tightness is common and should be distinguished from radicular pain.


Physical Examination
The physical examination findings often are normal or nonspecific. Decreased and
painful lumbar range of motion may be present. The step-off between the L4 and L5
spinous processes may be palpable in thin patients. A functional examination with
provocative testing may help rule out other etiologies, such as vascular claudication or
peripheral neuropathy.
The neurologic examination of patients with degenerative spondylolisthesis generally
does not contribute to the diagnosis, with patients often having normal motor
examination findings and preserved sensation and reflexes. Some patients with
substantial and long-standing spondylolisthesis have hamstring tightness.
In examining patients with degenerative spondylolisthesis, the physician should pay
utmost attention to ruling out other etiologies that may lead to claudication. Notably,
vascular claudication should always be kept in mind. Subtle clues, such as loss of hair,
decreased pedal pulses, and diminished sensation in the feet, should prompt additional
evaluation to rule out vascular disease or peripheral neuropathy.
Imaging Studies
Lateral upright radiographs, including flexion/extension views, should be obtained first.
MRI allows for assessment of the degree of spinal stenosis and may offer evidence regarding
the degree of instability.

Imaging Studies
The diagnosis of degenerative spondylolisthesis typically is based on upright lateral
lumbar spine radiographs.3 A dynamic slip may be missed if the physician relies on
supine radiographs. Therefore, upright radiographs are of primary importance, with
consideration also given to flexion/extension radiographs. Flexion and extension
radiographs may help differentiate stable spondylolisthesis from unstable

9/3/26, 4:35 PM
AAOS | Lumbar Degenerative Spondylolisthesis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003015
6/17

spondylolisthesis, with the distinction depending on the change in translation between
the views.4
MRI typically is the next step imaging modality used in the diagnosis and management of
degenerative spondylolisthesis. MRI is considered the preferred imaging modality to
evaluate the degree of spinal stenosis (Figure 3). In addition, MRI can help the clinician
predict the amount of instability. Factors that may indicate unstable degenerative
spondylolisthesis include increased disk height, increased fluid signal in the facet joints,
and sagittal orientation of the facet joint.5
In addition, comparing the amount of listhesis on a supine MRI and an upright lateral
radiograph may give the physician an idea of the amount of instability at that segment.

Figure 3 Sagittal T1-weighted MRI of the spine of a 70-year-old woman shows
spondylolisthesis at L4-L5. The disk signal changes at L4-L5 and L5-S1 are consistent with
the pathogenesis of degenerative spondylolisthesis. The listhesis has caused subsequent
thecal sac impingement. (Reproduced from Majid K, Fischgrund JS: Degenerative lumbar
spondylolisthesis: Trends in management. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2008;16[4]:208-215.)
Management
Nonsurgical Management
In the absence of neurologic deterioration, initial nonsurgical management is almost always
recommended. Treatment modalities include the following:
Activity modifications and weight loss
Smoking cessation6
NSAIDs
Physical therapy
Corticosteroid injections
Opioids are not a recommended treatment modality for degenerative spondylolisthesis.7

Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management is almost always recommended first. Behavioral changes,
including weight loss, increased physical activity, and smoking cessation, have been
found to lead to improved symptoms.
Although physical therapy is almost always prescribed, the effect of structured physical
therapy regimens is a subject of debate. A supervised physical therapy program focused
on improving lumbar spine strength was found to be more effective than home-based
programs.8
Corticosteroid injections include mainly epidural steroid injections, such as translaminar
and transforaminal injections. The long-term utility of epidural steroid injections in the
management of degenerative spondylolisthesis in patients with spinal stenosis is a
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:35 PM
AAOS | Lumbar Degenerative Spondylolisthesis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003015
8/17

subject of debate, and some evidence suggests that these treatment options may not be
more effective than placebo.9 Finally, the use of opioids in the management of
degenerative spondylolisthesis typically is not recommended because prolonged opioid
use may result in opioid-related adverse drug events and overuse, dependence, and
addiction.7
Surgical Management
Decompressive laminectomy
Laminectomy with instrumented fusion
Minimally invasive procedures
Surgical complications
Dural tear
Infection
Implant malpositioning
Adjacent segment disease

Surgical Management
Surgical treatment is recommended for patients who continue to experience symptoms
that interfere with their activities of daily living, despite appropriate nonsurgical
management for at least 3 months. Because of the various available surgical treatment
options, several factors must be taken considered before a surgical treatment option is
recommended. These factors include the pathology itself and patient-specific goals and
overall functional status.10
Occasionally, lumbar laminectomy is recommended in patients with static and stable
spondylolisthesis (Figure 4). Recommendations during laminectomy are to preserve at
least 8 mm of the pars interarticularis on both sides and to resect no more than 50% of
the facet joint. These recommendations are important to prevent iatrogenic
instability.11-13 A meta-analysis of the literature on decompression without fusion
indicates that 69% of patients treated via decompression alone had satisfactory

whether this progression resulted in poorer outcomes was unclear.
Figure 4 Images of the spine of a 67-year-old woman. AP (A) and lateral (B) radiographs
demonstrate stable degenerative spondylolisthesis at the L4-L5 segment. C, Midsagittal

Surgical management of lumbar degenerative spondylolisthesis. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2014;22[4]:203-213.)
Since the 1990s, evidence shows the advantages of fusion surgery in addition to
laminectomy in the management of spinal stenosis in patients with degenerative
spondylolisthesis.14 The addition of fusion is recommended in patients with dynamic
degenerative spondylolisthesis; in those patients, laminectomy alone may lead to
additional instability and recurrence of symptoms.10,15 A randomized controlled trial by
Försth et al16 showed that, in patients with lumbar stenosis with and without
degenerative spondylolisthesis, the addition of instrumented fusion did not lead to
improved outcomes at follow-up of 2 and 5 years. The groups with and without fusion
had comparable revision rates, and the fusion group had increased surgical time, blood
loss, and costs. A 2016 study by Ghogawala et al17 compared the effectiveness of
laminectomy alone versus laminectomy and instrumented fusion in patients with grade I
degenerative spondylolisthesis. The authors reported that laminectomy with fusion was
associated with slightly greater but clinically meaningful improvement in overall physical
health-related quality of life compared with laminectomy alone. The group that
underwent laminectomy alone had a higher revision rate than the fusion group during
the follow-up period (34% versus 14%). Better scores on the physical component of the
Medical Outcomes Study 36-Item Short Form were observed in the group that
underwent laminectomy plus fusion.17
The treatment of patients with multilevel stenosis and single-level spondylolisthesis is
controversial.18 Some surgeons think that decompression alone above or below a fused
level leads to additional stress, which may result in segmental instability.19,20 Therefore,
some surgeons recommend fusion of all decompressed levels, regardless whether they
are unstable. The counterargument is that multilevel fusion results in increased stress
on the adjacent levels, thereby increasing the incidence of adjacent segment disease.
Clinical evidence on this topic is scarce. In the Spine Patient Outcomes Research Trial,
many surgeons limited fusions to unstable levels only. Other surgeons performed longer

9/3/26, 4:35 PM
AAOS | Lumbar Degenerative Spondylolisthesis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003015
11/17

fusions to prevent instability at adjacent decompressed levels. A subgroup analysis
showed no clinically important differences between the two groups; however, patients
who underwent multilevel fusion had a higher rate of revision surgery.13
The addition of interbody fusion to posterior lumbar fusion is a subject of debate.
Proposed benefits of interbody fusion include graft placement along the weight-bearing
axis of the spine, improved spinal alignment and restoration of lumbar lordosis, and
improved reduction of spondylolisthesis.21,22
Although studies show improved radiographic fusion rates if interbody fusion is
performed in addition to posterolateral fusion, patient outcomes were not substantially
improved. In addition, some data show increased adjacent-segment degeneration at 5-
year follow-up.23
Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) techniques have been used for the management of
spinal stenosis and degenerative spondylolisthesis. These techniques include tubular
laminectomy and percutaneous placement of pedicle screws and interbody cages. The
benefits of MIS techniques include decreased blood loss and shorter hospital stays, and
the safety profile is similar to that of open techniques.24,25 A hurdle to the wide adoption
of MIS is the substantial learning curve necessary to master the technique.26,27 In
addition, no consensus has been reached on whether MIS fusion leads to improved
outcomes. Some studies show decreased postoperative pain, decreased blood loss,
shorter hospital length of stays, and faster recovery.28,29 Other studies did not show
clear benefits of MIS versus open techniques.30
A dural tear is one of the most common complications encountered during the surgical
management of degenerative spondylolisthesis. The incidence of incidental durotomy in
the literature ranges from 4% to 9%.31 Factors that increase the risk of durotomy include
facet joint cysts and severe stenosis.
Primary repair in a watertight fashion is considered the standard of care. Although
patients with incidental durotomy historically were thought to have poorer long-term
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:35 PM
AAOS | Lumbar Degenerative Spondylolisthesis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003015
12/17

outcomes, recent evidence shows that incidental durotomy did not have negative long-
term effects on patient outcomes.32
In the short term, revision surgery may be necessary for management of infection or
implant malpositioning. Long-term causes of the need for revision surgery include same-
segment disease, adjacent-segment disease, pseudarthrosis, and hardware-related pain.
Infections may be more prevalent in patients with extensive surgical dissections, obesity,
diabetes mellitus, or poor preoperative glycemic control. The use of instrumentation also
increases the risk for surgical site infection.
The rate of revision surgery in the management of same-segment disease was found to
be much higher in patients with degenerative spondylolisthesis who underwent
laminectomy alone compared with patients who underwent laminectomy and
instrumented fusion.33
Risk factors for adjacent-segment disease include higher body mass index, preoperative
degenerative changes of the disk space and the facet joints, and sagittal imbalance.34 In
addition, longer constructs lead to an increased incidence of adjacent-segment disease
and, therefore, increased long-term revision surgery rates.35
